artists.biography:
Desmond Dekker (16 July 1941 – 25 May 2006) was a Jamaican ska, rocksteady and reggae singer-songwriter and musician. Together with his backing group, The Aces (consisting of Wilson James and Easton Barrington Howard), he had one of the earliest international reggae hits with "Israelites" (1968). Other hits include "007 (Shanty Town)" (1967), "It Mek" (1969) and "You Can Get It If You Really Want" (1970).

The Aces
The current line-up for Dekker's backing band, who are still performing tribute concerts, includes:
Delroy Williams - backing vocals/M.C.
Gordon Mulrain - bass guitarist and session musician (Mulrain, also known as 'Innerheart', is co-founder of the British record label Ambiel Music)
Aubrey Mulrain - keyboard player and session musician
Steve Roberts - guitarist and session musician (also a member of the British band Dubzone)
Leroy Green - drums and session musician
Stan Samuel - guitarist and session musician
Charles Nelson - keyboard player and session musician
This particular line-up also recorded with Dekker on some of his later studio sessions in the 1990s.

perplexity.description:
Pretty Africa by Desmond Dekker & The Aces represents a collection of previously unreleased recordings from the early 1970s, capturing the artist during a prolific period of his reggae career. Recorded at Chalk Farm Studio in the summer of 1973, the album showcases Dekker's versatility across reggae and related styles, featuring tracks such as "Pretty Africa," "Treat Me Cruel," and "Love Is the Key." The material reflects the reggae sound that had established Dekker as an international figure following the success of earlier hits like "Israelites" and "You Can Get It If You Really Want."

The album's significance lies primarily in its archival value rather than contemporary commercial impact, as these recordings remained unreleased for decades before their official debut through Trojan Records in 2019. The tracks demonstrate Dekker's continued exploration of reggae themes and instrumentation during the early 1970s, a period when he was actively recording material that ranged from rude boy narratives to broader cultural commentary. While the original 1973 recordings did not receive commercial release at the time, the album's eventual publication provided listeners with insight into Dekker's studio work during a formative era of reggae's international expansion, complementing his established legacy as one of the genre's pioneering international ambassadors.
